rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 report the authors' own laboratory development and testing of a mobile variable-rate drip line (calibration curves, CUC tests, pressure-loss measurements).
rows.notes: The study contains no AI, predictive analytics, real-time weather or soil-moisture data; irrigation depths are pre-computed from ETo and Kc and loaded onto an SD card for an Arduino controller. The only water-conservation figure (Section 3.3: potential savings of 23.2%, at least 19.1%) is an arithmetic difference between average required and maximum depth in a lab bench test of variable-rate versus constant-rate drip, not a 30% reduction from AI-driven scheduling.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 report the authors' own laboratory tests of a mobile drip line (applied-depth measurements with collectors, CUC under constant and variable rates, speed and pressure-loss measurements).
rows.notes: The system is a drip line, but the only water-use result (Section 3.3, Figure 10: potential savings of 23.2% or at least 19.1%) is the calculated difference between variable-rate and constant-rate application under the same drip system, i.e. evidence about variable-rate control rather than about drip irrigation itself; it is a computed potential from a laboratory bench test with simulated crop demands, not a measured reduction in water use, and no IoT, AI or remote-sensing integration is present. The study's measured results concern uniformity (CUC 95-98%) and application efficiency (93.4%), not water conservation per se. Conclusions state that resource savings remain to be quantified.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 report the authors' own laboratory development and testing of a mobile variable-rate drip line.
rows.notes: No remote sensing is used; the only 'radio frequency' element is an NRF24L01 module for communication between two Arduino panels (Section 2.1). Required depths come from ETo and Kc tables (Table 1), not from sensing. Water savings (23.2%) are a calculated potential from variable-rate versus constant-rate drip application in the lab.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 report the authors' own laboratory development and testing of a mobile variable-rate drip line.
rows.notes: There is no app-based scheduling, IoT or AI; depths are pre-programmed on an SD card read by an Arduino Mega controller that sets line speed and valve pulse times (Sections 2, 2.1). The study shows that the developed drip line applies variable depths with CUC of about 95-98% and application efficiency of 93.4% in bench tests, and computes a potential saving of 23.2% versus constant-rate application; this is not evidence on app scheduling.

notes: Full text available; some pages are duplicated/garbled from PDF layout but content is readable. The study is a laboratory engineering evaluation of a mobile variable-rate drip line (uniformity, depth control, speed, pressure loss); it has no field crop trial, no sensors, IoT, AI or remote sensing, and its water-saving figure is a computed potential rather than a measured outcome.
